The past couple of weeks have been randomized rotation, frustration, and chop. You get traction for a few days and then it's gone. You have to be quick to rotate, act and react.

One thing stays consistent though. If you start system hopping or go way outside what you're used to doing, your results aren't going to reflect that the way you hope. Every time you change a strategy or change how you trade, there's a period where you're adapting to the new way of doing things.

For me that's always hurt more than it's helped.

When you add new components to your trading, take the time to master each one. If you're carrying too many pieces you haven't mastered and you're making it up on the fly, the outcomes get variable, random and frustrating.

Speaking to top traders over the past few years, they split about evenly on this.

Half of them swear by the psychological side. They've mastered pattern recognition, they can flip through charts and see it instantly, so what's left is managing themselves.

The other half says psychology is the excuse you reach for when you haven't studied enough. No scientific evidence it plays a role. Just study your setup until it's second nature.

My take is it's a bit of both. 

The longer you do this, the more patterns you've seen and the more cycles you've been through, the better you get. Maybe psychology matters less at that point. I agree with that.

But there's still the social media piece. I spoke to one trader this week who hasn't signed into Twitter since February. Doesn't want to see anyone else's opinion at all. For him that's the edge.

Some people improve by cutting out whatever hurts their psyche. Others by mastering every pattern and running it for 20 years straight. Do the same thing for two decades and of course you'll be good at it.

There's no right answer. It's whatever gets you to your end goal.

This past week in the Appalachians, away from screens, phones, the market & the constant noise of everyday life, has been one of the most refreshing weeks I’ve had in a long time.

I’m 22. I’ve been blessed to do well in business, and I’m not even remotely close to where I want to be, but being surrounded by nature, genuine community, and people serving others reminded me how little any $$ number on a screen actually means without people to share life with.

The markets have changed my life, and I LOVE the process of getting better at this business.

But something I’ve realized at a pretty young age is that the fulfillment comes WAY more from the person I’m becoming through my daily habits than whatever $$ happens to come from them. Money is an incredible tool, but meaningful relationships, family, community + using what I’ve been given to serve people who can’t give me anything in return mean infinitely more to me.

At the end of my life, nobody is going to care about my best trading month, how much money I made, or any of the material crap we spend so much time chasing.

I thank God every morning for what He’s entrusted me with, and I’m continually asking Him to teach me what it actually looks like to walk in humility, serve others well, and hold all of this with an open hand.

Thank you, Appalachians, for forcing me to slow down and reset before Q4. I’ve got a LOT to process and share from this week, but for now I’m just incredibly grateful. 

God is good. God bless!

Paul Tudor Jones :The Art of Aggressive Trading
Jack : What are the trading rules you live by?
PTJ: Don’t ever average losers. Decrease your trading volume when you are trading poorly; increase your volume when you are trading well. Never trade in situations where you don’t have control. For example, I don’t risk significant amounts of money in front of key reports, since that is gambling, not trading. If you have a losing position that is making you uncomfortable, the solution is very simple: Get out, because you can always get back in. There is nothing better than a fresh start.The most important rule of trading is to play great defense, not great offense. Every day I assume every position I have is wrong. I know where my stop risk points are going to be. I do that so I can define my maximum possible drawdown. Hopefully, I spend the rest of the day enjoying positions that are going in my direction. If they are going against me, then I have a game plan for getting out. Don’t be a hero. Don’t have an ego. Always question yourself and your ability. Don’t ever feel that you are very good. The second you do, you are dead. Jesse Livermore, one of the greatest speculators of all time, reportedly said that, in the long run, you can’t ever win trading markets. That was a devastating quote for someone like me, just getting into the business. The idea that you can’t beat the markets is a frightening prospect. That is why my guiding philosophy is playing great defense. If you make a good trade, don’t think it is because you have some uncanny foresight. Always maintain your sense of confidence, but keep it in check

Fair pushback, that tweet was too compressed. Here is the longer version, from the interview and from her public Kinfo trades (closed trades only).

The front end, as I understand it:

•find rich premium: high IV rank, implied above realized
•want structure: positive gamma, spot between the put wall and the call wall. Near the put wall she buys shares, in the middle she sells premium, near the call wall or in negative gamma she stands down
•want confirmation: bullish dark pool prints and call flow, Bookmap for timing
•sell 1 to 7 day puts about 2% OTM, one contract per ticket, take 50 to 90% of the premium, recycle

Her trades match that. About 1,900 short puts since mid-August 2025, median 3 DTE, median hold 24 hours, about 95% closed in profit.

My comment was about the back end: what happens when a put or a dip buy goes against her. She says it herself around 1:16. She doesn't cut, she becomes an investor. In the trades it looks like this:

•about half of the $1.41M in closed-trade profit came from shares, not options
•since mid-August 2025 she added at lower prices in 134 stock positions across 65 names. They made $259k, about half of the stock profit. Median hold 26 days
•of 527 stock positions held overnight, 89% closed in profit. Realized losses total $25k against $470k in gains. Largest single loss about $3k
•exits sit just above average cost. MSFT average $478, out at $496. META $701 and $727. TSLA $418 and $428. ORCL first buy $315, lowest $141, average $227, out at $232 after 248 days

A stock book that size with almost no realized losses means losers are held and added to until they come back. That's what I meant by averaging down in names she is willing to own, and it fits her own 8 to 9 month test.

Not a criticism. It has worked, and the selection layer is probably why the dips she buys tend to come back. But it is where the risk sits, and closed trades can't show positions that are still under water. Happy to be corrected if I'm misreading the data.

-  Background

In July of 2020, Matt Zambito (SqueezeMetrics) released a white paper titled The Implied Order Book.  It remains a sentinel piece.  Matt provided a Python Black-Scholes function to calculate how option deltas change in response to shifts in the underlying price (GEX) and implied volatility (VEX).  By scaling these sensitivities with Dealer Directional Open Interest (DDOI), Matt's script converted those sensitivities into dollar-volume and aggregated them to build an "implied order book" —revealing whether net market maker hedging leaned toward stabilizing liquidity (positive) or destabilizing volatility (negative).

In May of 2022, Cboe completed the rollout of 0DTE weekly options on SPX.  And with that, the modern options market was born.

-  nextSignals Upgrade

While daily expirations currently capture the lion's share of intraday liquidity, front-month regular options retain immense value for sentiment analysis because institutional investors still rely on them for large-scale positioning.  Consequently, these standard contracts act as a purer signal for institutional conviction and longer-term positioning, shielded from much of the retail-driven noise dominating daily contracts.

This weekend, I rebuilt SqueezeMetrics' GEX construction but pointed it at the near term:  sign every front-month print against the quote at time of trade and accumulate five sessions — market maker positioning measured off the tape, not assumed.  
A rolling 5-day ΔGEX ... is a reflection of bullish or bearish sentiment.
